column1: Where does control go when a catchable error occurs inside TRY?
column2:
To the associated CATCH block.
SQL Server skips the remaining statements in TRY and runs the matching CATCH. The error must be one that the block can catch.
Review source

column1: Where does control go after TRY finishes without an error?
column2:
To the statement after END CATCH.
SQL Server skips CATCH when nothing transfers control to it. Execution continues with the next statement after the construct.
Review source

column1: A CATCH block handles an error without throwing or returning. Where does execution normally continue?
column2:
After END CATCH.
Handling the error without rethrowing lets the batch continue. Use a return or throw if continuing would report false success.
Review source

column1: Why rethrow an unexpected caught error after cleanup?
column2:
The caller does not receive the caught exception automatically.
Cleanup and propagation are separate. A bare THROW sends the original failure to the enclosing caller after cleanup.
Review source

column1: Which compilation errors bypass TRY...CATCH at the same execution level?
column2:
Errors such as syntax errors that prevent the batch from running.
A same-level syntax error can prevent the block from compiling at all. An outer block can catch certain errors from a lower execution level.
Review source

column1: Which procedure can run a dynamic batch inside TRY so its missing-table error occurs at a lower execution level?
column2:
Execute that statement through sp_executesql inside TRY.
The dynamic statement compiles at a lower execution level. A missing-object error there can reach the TRY...CATCH around the call.
Review source

column1: What happens to local CATCH handling if an error closes the database connection?
column2:
It cannot run in that terminated connection.
There is no surviving session to execute local cleanup code. The client must handle the broken connection separately.
Review source

column1: How does TRY...CATCH treat a severity-10 informational message?
column2:
It does not transfer control to CATCH.
The message communicates information rather than a catchable failure. It does not skip the remaining TRY statements.
Review source

column1: Why can ERROR_MESSAGE() still report the original error after a successful logging statement in the same CATCH block?
column2:
Its value is scoped to the caught error.
The function reads the error associated with this CATCH, not a status from the most recent successful statement.
Review source

column1: What does ERROR_PROCEDURE return for a caught error raised outside any stored procedure or trigger?
column2:
NULL.
An ad hoc statement has no originating procedure or trigger name. Use other error information to locate the failure.
Review source

column1: If logging raises an error and enters its own nested CATCH, which error does ERROR_MESSAGE() describe there?
column2:
The error that invoked that CATCH.
An inner logging error can enter its own CATCH. That block's error details do not describe the original outer failure.
Review source

column1: What happens to the original error number when CATCH uses bare THROW;?
column2:
It is preserved.
For example, a caught constraint error keeps its system error number. Creating a new THROW message would use a new number.
Review source

column1: Why must logging precede bare THROW in a CATCH?
column2:
THROW transfers control, so later logging statements do not run.
Record the error details before rethrowing. Execution will not fall through to a logging statement afterward.
Review source

column1: Two THROW statements use the same error number. What can assigning a different state to each help you identify?
column2:
The location that raised the error.
For example, use the same error number for invalid input and a different state in each validation branch.
Review source

column1: Which function can prepare a formatted message for THROW?
column2:
FORMATMESSAGE.
Build the text first, then pass the resulting string to THROW. THROW does not directly substitute formatting arguments.
Review source

column1: Why must code using RAISERROR handle transaction rollback explicitly?
column2:
RAISERROR does not honor SET XACT_ABORT.
Raising the message does not apply the XACT_ABORT rule. Inspect the transaction and roll it back when required by the operation.
Review source

column1: What groups several data changes into an all-or-nothing operation?
column2:
An explicit transaction with appropriate commit and rollback handling.
Start a transaction before the related writes. Commit only when all required changes succeed, or roll back the unit.
Review source

column1: For a procedure-owned all-or-nothing transaction, when does the success path commit?
column2:
After all required operations succeed.
For example, commit an order and its line items only after both writes succeed. An earlier commit cannot be undone by a later rollback.
Review source

column1: In CATCH, @@TRANCOUNT is positive. Why is that not enough to decide whether SQL Server allows COMMIT?
column2:
It reports transaction count, not committability.
A positive count can coexist with XACT_STATE() = -1. Use XACT_STATE to distinguish an active transaction from a committable one.
Review source

column1: SET XACT_ABORT is ON. What transaction condition can still be present when control enters CATCH?
column2:
A caught error can leave an active transaction that cannot be committed.
Control can enter CATCH while SQL Server still holds a transaction open for rollback. Do not assume the setting already removed it.
Review source

column1: Which error phase is not covered by XACT_ABORT?
column2:
Compilation, including syntax errors.
The option applies to eligible run-time errors. It cannot change the handling of syntax errors that stop a batch from compiling.
Review source

column1: With XACT_ABORT OFF, what can happen after a statement-level runtime error?
column2:
Only the failed statement rolls back, leaving the transaction active.
Later statements can still run after certain statement failures. Use explicit error handling if earlier successful writes must also be undone.
Review source

column1: Why check for an active transaction before ROLLBACK in CATCH?
column2:
Some errors already roll back the transaction.
If the error already ended the transaction, another full ROLLBACK has nothing to roll back. Test the current state before cleanup.
Review source

column1: When XACT_STATE() returns -1, which kind of rollback can end the failed transaction?
column2:
A full transaction rollback, not a savepoint rollback.
The transaction cannot perform writes, and rolling back to a savepoint requires a log write. End it with a full rollback.
Review source

column1: A procedure owns a transaction that cannot commit. When can its handler write to an ordinary ErrorLog table?
column2:
After fully rolling back the failed transaction.
An ordinary log insert is a write and cannot run in an uncommittable transaction. After rollback, it can run outside that failed unit.
Review source

column1: If only the outer procedure started a shared transaction, which procedure coordinates a full rollback?
column2:
The outer procedure.
The outer procedure owns the transaction and decides whether to commit or roll back. Let an unexpected inner failure propagate to it.
Review source

column1: If @@TRANCOUNT is 2, what does ROLLBACK TRANSACTION without a savepoint do?
column2:
Rolls back the full transaction and sets @@TRANCOUNT to 0.
Nested BEGIN calls increase the count but do not create independently reversible transactions. A full rollback unwinds the entire unit.
Review source

column1: How can CATCH handle catchable errors from its own logging code?
column2:
Use a nested TRY...CATCH around the logging operation.
The inner CATCH can handle a logging failure without substituting it for the original error. Keep the original error details available.
Review source

column1: XACT_STATE() returns 1 after a required write fails. Why is that not enough to justify committing an all-or-nothing operation?
column2:
Committable does not mean every required operation succeeded.
Committable describes what SQL Server permits, not what the business operation accomplished. Roll back if a required step failed.
Review source
